items.title: Rates rise worldwide as government debt piles up
items.summary: Connects rising global bond yields to deficits and sovereign debt, and separates the level of spending from the budget balance when judging inflation.
items.lede: An ABC analysis argues investors are demanding higher returns to lend to governments, pushing up interest rates around the world, and that deficits, not just the size of spending, add to inflation. US interest payments on federal debt now exceed US$1 trillion a year and the Bank of England is tipped to raise its rate to 4.0%.
items.angle: Higher global yields raise borrowing costs for households, firms and governments, shifting AD left and easing the price level but cutting real GDP. Separate the level of spending from the budget balance when judging whether fiscal policy adds to inflation.
items.note: An analysis piece, so the claim that deficits drive inflation is one view. UPDATE DUE: RBA decision (3 November) and the Bank of England decision (5 November). Private data centre investment is also cited as an inflation pressure.

items.title: Albanese wants to rewrite part of the UK trade deal on backpackers
items.summary: Shows how a free trade agreement can cover labour mobility as well as tariffs, with winners and losers in the regional farm labour market.
items.lede: The Prime Minister will ask the UK to restore the regional work rule for British working holiday makers, which was waived under the Australia-UK free trade agreement. British backpackers rose from about 47,000 in 2024 to nearly 80,000 last financial year, and farmers warn of harvest labour shortages.
items.angle: Modern FTAs go beyond tariffs: services, investment and the movement of people all create winners and losers. The deal is already law, so changing it needs the UK's consent.
items.note: UPDATE DUE: outcome of the talks at CHOGM. The labour market diagram is the digest's illustration of a supply shift. The UK Prime Minister is named as Andy Burnham in the digest.

items.title: Commodity prices slip and the dollar softens before the RBA
items.summary: Shows how falling export prices lower demand for the AUD while a wider interest rate differential supports it. Replaces the 29 October edition.
items.lede: The Australian dollar slipped 0.1% to 70.20 US cents on 2 November as iron ore held at US$90.80 a tonne and copper fell 1.5%, ahead of the expected RBA rate rise. Australia's 10-year bond yield of 5.13% is above the US 4.93%, which supports demand for AUD assets.
items.angle: Lower commodity prices mean foreign buyers need fewer Australian dollars for our exports, shifting AUD demand left. An RBA hike works the other way: a wider differential attracts capital inflows and shifts demand right.
items.note: Single-day figures, so update before quoting. UPDATE DUE: RBA decision on 3 November. Replaces the 29 October edition; the 28 October item on the NZ dollar is kept.

items.title: House prices fall at the fastest pace in 40 years
items.summary: The October Cotality result: a seventh monthly fall, with the wealth effect and transmission of higher rates. Replaces the sixth-month edition.
items.lede: National home values fell 1.2% in October, the seventh straight monthly fall, and are 6.7% below the March peak, about $63,400 off the median dwelling. Capital cities are down 8.1% in seven months and set to pass the 2017-19 record fall of 8.2%, and AMP now expects a 15% fall.
items.angle: Higher rates cut borrowing capacity and investors have pulled back after property tax changes, shifting housing demand left. Falling prices hit recent buyers with small deposits hardest, which matters for wealth distribution as well as spending.
items.note: Replaces the sixth-month item, which reported HSBC's economist expecting falls of up to 13%. The AMP forecast is one institution's view. See also the 25 October Domain quarterly figures.

items.title: Inflation pressures persist as factories contract
items.summary: A timely monthly inflation gauge and PMI, with the Phillips curve diagram showing why rising expectations make disinflation costlier.
items.lede: The Melbourne Institute Inflation Gauge rose 0.5% in October (September 0.3%), its fourth straight monthly rise, while the manufacturing PMI fell to 49.6, its second month of contraction. The ABS reported headline CPI of 4.3% and trimmed mean of 3.6% for the year to September.
items.angle: If people expect higher inflation, the short-run Phillips curve shifts out, so inflation rises even as unemployment rises and getting back to 2-3% becomes more costly. This is why the RBA targets underlying inflation and acts early to anchor expectations.
items.note: The Melbourne Institute gauge is a private monthly estimate, not an official statistic. UPDATE DUE: RBA decision on 3 November.

items.title: Oil eases on Hormuz talks, but the supply shock is not over
items.summary: Shows how a possible reopening of the Strait of Hormuz shifts oil supply back, while a geopolitical risk premium keeps prices high. Replaces the 30 October edition.
items.lede: Brent crude fell about 2-3% on 2 November to around US$108-111 a barrel after rising 14-15% in October and peaking near US$118, as Iran held talks in Qatar on reopening the strait. Goldman Sachs estimates about US$27 a barrel is a geopolitical risk premium.
items.angle: Short-run oil demand is inelastic, so a supply cut raises the price a lot. A deal that reopens the strait would shift supply back right. On an AD/AS diagram the shock shifts SRAS left: higher prices and lower output, or stagflation.
items.note: Replaces the 30 October item, which reported Brent settling at US$117.64 and at least 35 attacks on shipping in October; that report put the Hormuz traffic about 70% below pre-war levels. Iran set conditions for reopening, including an end to the US naval blockade. UPDATE DUE: outcome of the talks.

items.title: House prices record their biggest quarterly fall: down 4.7% in the September quarter
items.summary: The largest quarterly fall in house prices on record, with the wealth effect and asset price channel of monetary policy.
items.lede: Domain data show the national median house price fell 4.7% in the September quarter, the largest quarterly drop on record and the first time in 15 years that prices fell in every capital city. Regional South Australia rose 6.3% in the quarter and 19% over the year.
items.angle: Housing is most households' main asset, so falling prices reduce wealth. The effect on the distribution of wealth is not clear-cut: affordability improves for buyers who can still borrow at higher rates.
items.note: Domain median prices are one measure of the market. One economist expects falls to continue for another 6 to 12 months. See also the monthly Cotality figures filed on 2 November.

items.title: Banks see slower growth and higher unemployment, but still expect a hike
items.summary: A current stagflation example: NAB and CBA cut growth to about 1% and lifted unemployment forecasts while inflation stays above target.
items.lede: NAB cut its 2027 GDP growth forecast to 1.0% and expects unemployment to reach 5.4% by the end of 2027, while CBA cut growth to about 1% by mid-2027 from 1.8% and raised its unemployment forecast to 5.1% from 4.8%. CBA expects trimmed mean inflation to stay at or above 3.5% until at least mid-2027.
items.angle: Higher fuel and construction costs shift SRAS left, so prices rise while output falls. Raising rates to fight supply-driven inflation deepens the slowdown, a key limitation of monetary policy.
items.note: Bank forecasts are projections, not outcomes, and the digest relies on an ABC live blog summary. The "stagflation" label is the digest's description. UPDATE DUE: RBA forecasts on 3 November.

items.title: Could government spending cuts do the RBA's job?
items.summary: Compares contractionary fiscal policy with a rate rise as ways to reduce inflation, with Chris Richardson's rule of thumb.
items.lede: With a fifth rate rise for the year expected, economists and politicians are debating whether the budget should do more of the work of bringing inflation down. Chris Richardson estimates that $7-10 billion a year in spending cuts would have about the same effect as one rate rise.
items.angle: Evaluate both arms: fiscal policy can be targeted but is slow and political, while monetary policy is flexible but blunt and falls mainly on borrowers. If the budget does more, the RBA may need to do less.
items.note: The Richardson estimate is a rule of thumb, not a precise forecast. The Opposition named the home battery program and EV discount as possible cuts; that is its proposal. UPDATE DUE: RBA decision on 3 November.
